source_refs.note: Exercise 1.4, Question 1: book p. 28, Q1 (i)-(vi) exponential and logarithmic equations; answer key book p. 299 (PDF 301)

blocks.explanation:
A logarithmic equation with one logarithm on each side, both to base 10.
Plan: find the domain, equate the arguments (log is one-to-one), solve the quadratic, and keep only the roots inside the domain.
steps:
Given: \(\log(3x - 2) = \log(x^2 - 5x + 6)\).
To find: all real solutions \(x\).
Method: the logarithm is one-to-one, so equal logarithms (same base) have equal arguments. The domain decides which roots survive.

Domain
\[3x - 2 > 0 \Rightarrow x > \tfrac{2}{3}\]
\[x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3) > 0\]
\[\Rightarrow x < 2 \text{ or } x > 3\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]\tfrac{2}{3}, 2[ \cup ]3, \infty[\]
Why: each logarithm needs a positive argument, and both conditions must hold together.

Equate the arguments
\[3x - 2 = x^2 - 5x + 6\]
\[x^2 - 8x + 8 = 0\]
Why: \(\log u = \log v \iff u = v\).

Quadratic formula
\[x = \dfrac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 - 32}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 \pm 4\sqrt{2}}{2} = 4 \pm 2\sqrt{2}\]
Why: \(a = 1,\ b = -8,\ c = 8\) and \(\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\).

Compare with the domain
\(4 - 2\sqrt{2} \approx 1.17\) lies in \(]\frac{2}{3}, 2[\): accepted.
\(4 + 2\sqrt{2} \approx 6.83\) lies in \(]3, \infty[\): accepted.
Why: a root is a solution only if both logarithms exist there.

Check:
At \(x = 4 - 2\sqrt{2}\):
\[3x - 2 = 10 - 6\sqrt{2} \approx 1.51 > 0\]
Both arguments are equal at each root (that is how the roots were found), so it is enough that one of them is positive.

blocks.explanation:
The same type as part (i), now with natural logarithms.
Plan: domain, equate the arguments, solve the quadratic, reject the root outside the domain.
steps:
Given: \(\ln(x^2 - 1) = \ln(3x - 2)\).
To find: all real solutions \(x\).
Method: \(\ln\) is one-to-one, so the arguments are equal; then check the domain.

Domain
\[x^2 - 1 > 0 \Rightarrow x < -1 \text{ or } x > 1\]
\[3x - 2 > 0 \Rightarrow x > \tfrac{2}{3}\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]1, \infty[\]
Why: both arguments must be positive; the common part of the two conditions is \(x > 1\).

Equate the arguments
\[x^2 - 1 = 3x - 2\]
\[x^2 - 3x + 1 = 0\]
Why: \(\ln u = \ln v \iff u = v\).

Quadratic formula
\[x = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 4}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}\]
Why: \(a = 1,\ b = -3,\ c = 1\).

Compare with the domain
\(\frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 2.618 > 1\): accepted.
\(\frac{3 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 0.382\) is not greater than 1: rejected.
Why: at \(x \approx 0.382\), \(3x - 2 \approx -0.854 < 0\), so \(\ln(3x - 2)\) does not exist.

Check:
At \(x = \frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\), \(x^2 = 3x - 1\), so
\[x^2 - 1 = 3x - 2 \approx 5.854 > 0 \;\checkmark\]

blocks.explanation:
Two logarithms on the left, one on the right.
Plan: domain, product law on the left, equate the arguments, solve the cubic by factorising.
steps:
Given: \(\log(x) + \log(x^2 - 5x + 7) = \log(3)\).
To find: all real solutions \(x\).
Method: join the left side into one logarithm with the product law, then equate arguments (one-to-one).

Domain
\[x > 0\]
\[x^2 - 5x + 7 = \left(x - \tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{3}{4} > 0\]
\[\text{Domain} = ]0, \infty[\]
Why: completing the square shows the second argument is always positive, so only \(x > 0\) matters.

Product law and equate arguments
\[\log[x(x^2 - 5x + 7)] = \log 3\]
\[x^3 - 5x^2 + 7x = 3\]
\[x^3 - 5x^2 + 7x - 3 = 0\]
Why: \(\log m + \log n = \log(mn)\), then \(\log u = \log v \iff u = v\).

Factorise the cubic
\[x^3 - x^2 - 4x^2 + 4x + 3x - 3\]
\[= (x - 1)(x^2 - 4x + 3)\]
\[= (x - 1)^2(x - 3)\]
Why: the coefficients add to \(1 - 5 + 7 - 3 = 0\), so \(x = 1\) is a root and \((x - 1)\) is a factor.

Roots and domain
\(x = 1\) (repeated) or \(x = 3\). Both are positive, so both are in the domain.

Check:
\(x = 1\): \(\log 1 + \log 3 = 0 + \log 3 = \log 3\) \(\checkmark\)
\(x = 3\): \(\log 3 + \log 1 = \log 3\) \(\checkmark\)

blocks.explanation:
An exponential equation with \(3^{x+1}\) and \(9^x\): both are powers of 3.
Plan: put \(y = 3^x\), solve the quadratic in \(y\), reject the negative value, then find \(x\).
steps:
Given: \(3^{(x+1)} - 2 \cdot 9^x + 9 = 0\).
To find: all real solutions \(x\).
Method: write everything in terms of \(3^x\); the substitution \(y = 3^x\) turns it into a quadratic.

Domain
\[\text{Domain} = ]-\infty, \infty[\]
Why: exponentials are defined for every real number.

Substitute \(y = 3^x\) (\(y > 0\))
\[3y - 2y^2 + 9 = 0\]
\[2y^2 - 3y - 9 = 0\]
\[(y - 3)(2y + 3) = 0\]
Why: multiplying by \(-1\) makes the leading term positive; \(2y^2 - 6y + 3y - 9\) splits the middle term.

Reject the impossible value
\(y = -\frac{3}{2}\): impossible, because \(3^x > 0\) for every \(x\).
\[3^x = 3 = 3^1 \Rightarrow x = 1\]
Why: one-to-one property of the exponential function.

blocks.explanation:
A logarithmic equation to base \(\frac{1}{e}\) with \(x\) as a multiplier on the left.
As printed (\(16^3\)) it does not lead to the key's answer; the intended right side is \(\log_{\frac{1}{e}}(16^x - 3)\) (see the correction below).
Plan: power law on the left, equate arguments, then \(y = 4^x\) gives a quadratic.
steps:
Given (intended form): \(x\log_{\frac{1}{e}} 4 = \log_{\frac{1}{e}}(16^x - 3)\).
To find: the real solution \(x\).
Method: the power law moves \(x\) into the exponent, \(x\log_a 4 = \log_a 4^x\). Then both sides are logarithms to the same base, so the arguments are equal. Since \(16^x = (4^x)^2\), the substitution \(y = 4^x\) gives a quadratic.

Domain
\[16^x - 3 > 0 \Rightarrow 16^x > 3\]
Why: the argument of a logarithm must be positive. The base \(\frac{1}{e}\) is positive and not 1, so it is allowed.

Power law on the left
\[\log_{\frac{1}{e}}(4^x) = \log_{\frac{1}{e}}(16^x - 3)\]
Why: \(k\log_a u = \log_a u^k\).

Equate the arguments
\[4^x = 16^x - 3\]
Why: a logarithm with any allowed base is one-to-one.

Substitute \(y = 4^x\) (\(y > 0\))
\[16^x = (4^2)^x = (4^x)^2 = y^2\]
\[y = y^2 - 3\]
\[y^2 - y - 3 = 0\]
Why: \(16^x\) and \(4^x\) are linked through the same base 4.

Solve the quadratic
\[y = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 12}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}\]
Why: \(a = 1,\ b = -1,\ c = -3\).

Reject the negative value
\(\frac{1 - \sqrt{13}}{2} \approx -1.30 < 0\): impossible for \(4^x\).
\(\frac{1 + \sqrt{13}}{2} \approx 2.303\): accepted.
Why: \(4^x > 0\) for every real \(x\).

Find \(x\)
\[4^x = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{13}}{2}\]
\[x = \log_4\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{13}}{2}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\log_2\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{13}}{2}\right)\]
Why: \(\log_4 u = \frac{\log_2 u}{\log_2 4} = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 u\) (change of base). Numerically \(x \approx 0.6017\).

Check:
\[16^x = y^2 = y + 3 \approx 5.303 > 3\]
so \(x\) is in the domain, and \(16^x - 3 = y = 4^x\), so both sides are equal \(\checkmark\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the right side as \(\log_{\frac{1}{e}}(16^3 - 3)\). With \(16^3\) the equation becomes \(4^x = 16^3 - 3 = 4093\), so \(x = \log_4 4093 \approx 5.9995\), which does not match the answer key. The key's answer \(\frac{1}{2}\log_2\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{13}}{2}\right)\) is the solution of \(x\log_{\frac{1}{e}} 4 = \log_{\frac{1}{e}}(16^x - 3)\), so the exponent 3 is a misprint for \(x\). We solved the intended equation.

blocks.explanation:
An exponential equation with \(2^x\) and \(2^{-x} = \frac{1}{2^x}\).
Plan: put \(y = 2^x\), clear the fraction, solve the quadratic, then take \(\log_2\).
steps:
Given: \(2^x + 2^{-x} = 5\).
To find: all real solutions \(x\).
Method: \(2^{-x} = \frac{1}{2^x}\), so with \(y = 2^x\) the equation becomes \(y + \frac{1}{y} = 5\), a quadratic after multiplying by \(y\).

Domain
\[\text{Domain} = ]-\infty, \infty[\]
Why: exponentials are defined for every real number.

Substitute \(y = 2^x\) (\(y > 0\))
\[y + \dfrac{1}{y} = 5\]
\[y^2 + 1 = 5y\]
\[y^2 - 5y + 1 = 0\]
Why: multiplying by \(y > 0\) clears the fraction and changes nothing else.

Quadratic formula
\[y = \dfrac{5 \pm \sqrt{25 - 4}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{5 \pm \sqrt{21}}{2}\]
Why: \(a = 1,\ b = -5,\ c = 1\).

Both values are positive
\(\sqrt{21} \approx 4.58 < 5\), so both \(\frac{5 \pm \sqrt{21}}{2}\) are positive and both are accepted.
\[x = \log_2\left(\dfrac{5 + \sqrt{21}}{2}\right) \approx 2.2604\]
\[x = \log_2\left(\dfrac{5 - \sqrt{21}}{2}\right) \approx -2.2604\]
Why: \(2^x = c \iff x = \log_2 c\) for \(c > 0\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{5 + \sqrt{21}}{2} \cdot \dfrac{5 - \sqrt{21}}{2} = \dfrac{25 - 21}{4} = 1\]
so the two roots are negatives of each other, as expected: replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) does not change \(2^x + 2^{-x}\). Also \(4.791 + 0.209 = 5\) \(\checkmark\)
